books.title: The Lost Key
books.author: ODAK
books.description: Maya anahtarını kaybeder ve bir gün boyunca mahallesindeki insanları tanır. Kısa cümleler, günlük kelimeler.

sections.title: A Bad Morning
paragraphs: Maya lives in a small flat on Park Street. She works in a bakery near the station. Every morning she gets up at six, drinks a cup of tea and leaves the house at seven.

On Monday morning, Maya was late. She took her bag and her coat and ran down the stairs. When she got to the street, she stopped. It was cold and it was raining. She wanted her umbrella, so she went back to her door.
She looked in her bag for her key. It was not there. She looked in her coat. It was not there. She looked in her bag again, but she only found a pen, a phone and an old bus ticket.
"Oh no," she said. "Where is my key?"

sections.title: The Neighbours
paragraphs: Maya knocked on the next door. An old man opened it. His name was Mr. Aydin, but Maya did not know that. She lived next to him for two years, but they never talked.
"Good morning," she said. "I'm your neighbour. I lost my key. Can I use your phone? My phone has no battery."
"Of course," said the old man. "Come in. You are wet. Would you like some tea?" Maya looked at her watch. She was already late, but she was also very cold. "Yes, please," she said.

They sat in the small kitchen. Mr. Aydin told her about his garden on the roof. Maya told him about the bakery. He laughed and said, "So you are the person who makes that wonderful bread! I buy it every Saturday."

sections.title: Found
paragraphs: Maya called her boss and explained the problem. Then she went to the station to ask about her key. The woman at the desk was friendly. She looked in a big box, but there were only gloves and hats in it.
In the evening, Maya walked home slowly. She was tired and she still had no key. Then she saw Mr. Aydin at the door of the building. He was smiling, and he had something in his hand.
"I went up to my garden," he said. "I found this next to the stairs. Is it yours?" It was her key. It fell out of her bag that morning when she ran.
Maya was very happy. The next Saturday, she took a large loaf of bread to his door. Now they drink tea together every week, and she never runs down the stairs.

books.title: A New City
books.author: ODAK
books.description: Can işi için İngiltere'de küçük bir şehre taşınır. Yeni bir hayata alışmanın küçük başarıları.

sections.title: The First Week
paragraphs: Can is twenty-six years old and he is from Izmir. Last month he got a new job at a hospital in York, a small city in the north of England. He was excited, but he was also afraid. His English was not very good and he did not know anybody.

On his first day, he took the wrong bus. He arrived at work forty minutes late. His manager, Helen, did not get angry. "Everybody takes the wrong bus here," she said. "The numbers are very confusing."
In the evenings, Can was alone in his room. He called his mother and told her that everything was fine. It was not completely true. He missed his family, the sea and the food.

sections.title: Small Words
paragraphs: People in York spoke fast. They also used words that Can did not learn at school. In a shop, a woman called him "love". He felt embarrassed until a colleague explained that it was just a friendly word.
Can started to write new words in a small notebook. Every day he wrote five words and used them at work. Some days he made mistakes and people smiled, but they always helped him.
After a month, he understood more. He could talk on the phone without being nervous. One morning a patient said, "You speak very well. Where are you from?" Can felt proud all day.

sections.title: Home
paragraphs: In spring, Helen invited the team to her house for dinner. Everybody brought some food. Can made his mother's rice with vegetables. He was nervous, but the plate was empty in ten minutes.
"You must teach me how to make this," Helen said. Later that night, Can walked home by the river. The air was warm and the old walls of the city were beautiful.
He called his mother again. "How is everything?" she asked. This time, he did not need to lie. "It's good," he said. "It's really good."

books.title: The Lighthouse Keeper
books.author: ODAK
books.description: Genç bir araştırmacı, kapanmak üzere olan bir deniz fenerinin son bekçisiyle tanışır. Sakin bir dille yalnızlık ve görev üzerine.

sections.title: The Island
paragraphs: The boat left Elena on the island at noon and turned back immediately, because the captain wanted to reach the harbour before the weather changed. She stood on the small wooden pier with her bag and watched it disappear into the grey water.

She had come to write a report for the government. The lighthouse was going to be closed at the end of the year, and someone needed to record what was there before everything was removed. It was supposed to be an easy job that would take two days.

An old man was waiting at the top of the path. He did not offer to carry her bag. "You're the one from the ministry," he said. It did not sound like a question. His name was Thomas, and he had been the keeper for forty-one years.

sections.title: The Logbooks
paragraphs: Inside the lighthouse, the air smelled of oil and old paper. Thomas showed her a room full of logbooks. Every night for more than a hundred years, a keeper had written down the weather, the ships and anything unusual that had happened.

Elena opened one at random. The handwriting was neat and careful. "Heavy fog. Bell rung for six hours. Fishing boat came in safely at dawn." She turned the page. "Clear night. Nothing to report." She read for much longer than she had planned.

"Why do you still write them?" she asked. "Ships have satellite navigation now. Nobody is going to read these." Thomas thought about this while he cleaned his glasses. "You are reading them," he said.

sections.title: The Storm
paragraphs: The storm arrived that evening, earlier than anyone had predicted. No boat could come for at least three days. Elena tried to be annoyed, but she found that she did not really mind. She helped Thomas carry wood and learned how the great lamp worked.

On the second night, the radio woke them. A small sailing boat had lost its engine somewhere to the north, and its navigation system had stopped working. The man on the radio was young and sounded frightened. All he could see, he said, was a light.

Thomas climbed the stairs slowly. He checked the lamp, although it did not need checking, and he stayed beside it until morning. At dawn the radio spoke again: the boat was safe in the bay. Thomas opened the logbook and wrote one line.

sections.title: The Report
paragraphs: When Elena returned to the city, she sat in her office for a long time with her report open on the screen. The numbers were clear. The lighthouse was expensive, and the technology had made it almost unnecessary.

She wrote everything that was true. Then she added a final page that nobody had asked for. It described a clear night and a frightened voice on the radio, and it asked whether a system that always works is the same as one that someone is watching.

She never found out if anyone read that page. But the following spring, a postcard arrived with a picture of the island on the front. On the back there were only four words, in neat and careful handwriting: "Clear night. Light on."

books.title: The Last Train North
books.author: ODAK
books.description: Kaçırılan bir tren, iki yabancı ve uzun bir gece. Geçmiş zaman ve diyalog alıştırması için akıcı bir hikâye.

sections.title: Platform Nine
paragraphs: Daniel reached platform nine at exactly the moment the doors closed. He knocked on the window, but the train had already started to move. He stood there breathing hard and looking at the red lights as they became smaller. It was the last train north, and his sister's wedding was at ten o'clock the next morning.

"You could try running faster," said a voice behind him. A woman of about sixty was sitting on a bench with a large suitcase. She had also missed the train, she explained, but she had done it on purpose. Daniel did not understand, and she did not explain.

sections.title: The Car
paragraphs: Her name was Ruth. She had an old car in the station car park, and she was going north anyway. "I was going to take the train because I hate driving at night," she said. "But I'm also afraid of what's waiting at the end of the journey, so I sat on that bench for an hour."

Daniel offered to drive. Rain began to fall as they left the city. For a long time neither of them spoke. Then Ruth asked him about the wedding, and he found himself telling her about his sister, about their argument two years ago, and about the message he had almost not answered.

"What did you argue about?" Ruth asked. Daniel tried to remember the exact reason. It had seemed extremely important at the time. "Money, I think," he said at last. "Or perhaps about who had called whom last." Ruth laughed quietly.

sections.title: The House by the Lake
paragraphs: Just before sunrise, they stopped by a lake so that Ruth could stretch her legs. She told him then why she was travelling. Her brother lived in a house on the other side of the water. They had not spoken for twenty-three years, and last week a doctor had told him that he did not have much time.

"I've been practising what to say since Tuesday," she said. "It's a very good speech. There are several excellent points in it." She looked at the water for a moment. "I think I'm going to throw it away."

Daniel got to the wedding with eleven minutes to spare, wearing a borrowed jacket. His sister saw him from across the room and began to cry, and so he never needed the speech he had prepared either. A week later a card arrived with no return address. It said only: "I didn't throw away all of it. He laughed at the third point."

books.title: Sleep and Memory
books.author: ODAK
books.description: Uyku sırasında beyinde neler olur, sınavdan önceki gece neden önemlidir? YÖKDİL Sağlık metinlerine yakın bir okuma.

sections.title: Why We Sleep
paragraphs: For most of human history, sleep was regarded as a passive state, a period in which the body and mind simply switched off. Modern research has shown that this view is mistaken. During sleep, the brain remains remarkably active, and much of this activity appears to serve a specific purpose: the organisation and storage of information acquired during the day.

Sleep is not a single, uniform condition. It consists of repeating cycles, each lasting roughly ninety minutes, in which the sleeper moves through light sleep, deep slow-wave sleep and rapid eye movement (REM) sleep. The proportion of each stage changes through the night, with deep sleep concentrated in the early hours and REM sleep becoming longer towards morning.

sections.title: From Short-Term to Long-Term
paragraphs: New memories are initially fragile. They depend heavily on the hippocampus, a small structure deep inside the brain that acts as a temporary store. Over time, these memories must be transferred to the cortex, where they can be held more permanently. This gradual process is known as consolidation.

Studies suggest that deep sleep plays a central role in this transfer. Recordings from animal and human brains show that patterns of activity seen during learning are replayed, at much higher speed, during slow-wave sleep. Participants who are deprived of this stage after studying a list of words typically remember significantly fewer of them the following day, even when they are given extra time to rest.

REM sleep seems to contribute in a different way. Although the evidence is less conclusive, it has been associated with emotional memory and with the ability to find connections between ideas that were not obviously related. Consequently, a full night's sleep may help a person not only to recall facts but also to understand them.

sections.title: The Night Before an Exam
paragraphs: These findings have an obvious practical implication for students. Staying awake all night to study may increase the amount of material a person has seen, but it reduces the amount that can be retained. Moreover, sleep deprivation impairs attention and working memory, both of which are essential for reading complex passages under time pressure.

This does not mean that sleep can replace study. Consolidation can only strengthen what has already been encoded, and material that was never properly learned will not appear by magic in the morning. The most effective approach appears to be distributed practice: shorter study sessions spread over several days, each followed by a normal night of sleep.

Researchers also caution against exaggerated claims. Individual needs vary considerably, and a single poor night is unlikely to cause serious harm. Nevertheless, the general conclusion is well supported: for most adults, seven to nine hours of sleep is not time lost from learning, but part of the learning process itself.

books.title: Vaccines Explained
books.author: ODAK
books.description: Aşıların bağışıklık sistemini nasıl eğittiği, sürü bağışıklığı ve yan etkiler. Sağlık metinlerinde sık geçen terimlerle.

sections.title: Training the Immune System
paragraphs: When a virus or bacterium enters the body for the first time, the immune system needs several days to respond effectively. During this period, the infection can spread and cause serious illness. Once the threat has been defeated, however, the body retains a population of memory cells that can recognise the same pathogen and react quickly if it returns.

A vaccine exploits this mechanism. By presenting the immune system with a harmless version or fragment of a pathogen, it stimulates the production of antibodies and memory cells without causing the disease itself. If the vaccinated person later encounters the real pathogen, the body is already prepared, and the infection is either prevented or considerably reduced in severity.

sections.title: Different Types of Vaccine
paragraphs: Vaccines are produced in several ways. Some contain a live but weakened form of the organism, which tends to produce strong and lasting immunity but may be unsuitable for people with weakened immune systems. Others contain inactivated organisms or only a single protein taken from the surface of the pathogen; these are generally safer, although they often require booster doses.

More recent technologies use genetic instructions, delivered in the form of messenger RNA or through a harmless carrier virus, which cause the body's own cells to produce a viral protein for a short time. Because such vaccines can be designed quickly once the genetic sequence of a pathogen is known, they have become particularly valuable during outbreaks.

sections.title: Protection Beyond the Individual
paragraphs: Vaccination protects more than the person who receives it. When a sufficiently large proportion of a population is immune, a pathogen has difficulty finding new hosts and its transmission slows. This effect, known as herd immunity, indirectly protects those who cannot be vaccinated, such as very young infants and certain patients undergoing medical treatment.

The required proportion depends on how contagious a disease is. For measles, one of the most infectious diseases known, coverage of around ninety-five percent is needed. As a result, even a modest decline in vaccination rates can allow outbreaks to occur in communities where the disease had previously disappeared.

sections.title: Weighing Risks and Benefits
paragraphs: Like all medical interventions, vaccines can have side effects. Most are mild and short-lived, such as a sore arm or a slight fever, and they usually indicate that the immune system is responding. Serious reactions do occur, but they are rare, and safety systems continue to monitor vaccines long after they have been approved.

Public debate often focuses on these rare events because they are visible, whereas the illnesses that vaccines prevent have become invisible precisely because vaccination has been so successful. When the risks are compared directly, most health authorities conclude that the benefits of recommended vaccines far outweigh their potential harms.

books.title: Cities and Climate
books.author: ODAK
books.description: Şehirler neden çevresinden daha sıcaktır, iklim değişikliğine nasıl uyum sağlar? YÖKDİL Fen metinlerine uygun bir okuma.

sections.title: The Urban Heat Island
paragraphs: On a summer evening, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the countryside only a few kilometres away. This phenomenon, known as the urban heat island effect, was first described in the nineteenth century, but it has become increasingly significant as more of the world's population has moved to cities.

Several factors contribute to the effect. Asphalt and concrete absorb solar radiation during the day and release it slowly at night. Tall buildings trap this heat and reduce wind speed, while the scarcity of trees limits the cooling that plants provide through evaporation. In addition, vehicles and air conditioning systems release waste heat directly into the surrounding air.

sections.title: Why It Matters
paragraphs: Higher urban temperatures are more than a matter of discomfort. During heatwaves, the lack of cooling at night prevents the body from recovering, and mortality rises sharply, particularly among the elderly and those with chronic illnesses. Demand for electricity also increases, which can place heavy strain on power networks and, where fossil fuels are used, produce further emissions.

Importantly, the risks are not distributed equally. Poorer neighbourhoods frequently have fewer trees, denser housing and less access to air conditioning. Studies from several countries have found that temperature differences within a single city may be as large as those between the city and its rural surroundings.

sections.title: Designing Cooler Cities
paragraphs: Cities are not merely victims of climate change; they are also places where effective solutions can be applied at scale. Planting street trees provides shade and evaporative cooling, while parks and green corridors can lower temperatures in surrounding districts. Roofs and pavements coated with reflective materials absorb less sunlight, and in some climates they have reduced peak temperatures measurably.

Such measures usually bring additional benefits. Green spaces absorb rainwater and thereby reduce the risk of flooding, and they are associated with improved mental health. However, trees need water and years of growth, and reflective surfaces may increase glare, so no single approach is suitable everywhere.

The challenge, therefore, is one of planning as much as of technology. Decisions made today about land use, transport and building design will shape urban temperatures for decades. Since most of the cities that will exist in 2050 have not yet been fully built, there remains a considerable opportunity to design them differently.

books.title: How Languages Change
books.author: ODAK
books.description: Dil neden değişir, kim karar verir, bir dil neden ölür? YÖKDİL Sosyal metinlerine yakın, ilgi çekici bir okuma.

sections.title: No Language Stands Still
paragraphs: Anyone who has tried to read Shakespeare without notes knows that English has changed considerably in four hundred years. Yet speakers rarely notice such changes as they happen. Because each generation learns language from the previous one with only slight differences, the process is slow and largely invisible, much like the movement of the hour hand on a clock.

Change affects every level of language. Pronunciation shifts, grammatical endings disappear, and the meanings of words move in unexpected directions. The English word nice, for instance, once meant foolish, and it passed through several other senses before arriving at its current pleasant meaning.

sections.title: Why Change Happens
paragraphs: Linguists have identified several causes. Contact between speakers of different languages is among the most powerful, since words and sometimes grammatical structures are readily borrowed. English, after the Norman conquest of 1066, absorbed thousands of French words, which is why it often has pairs such as begin and commence.

Social factors are equally important. People tend to adjust their speech to resemble those whose group they wish to belong to, and younger speakers often adopt new forms as a way of marking their identity. Although older generations commonly regard these innovations as errors, many forms that were once criticised are now considered perfectly standard.

sections.title: Do Rules Matter?
paragraphs: Many countries have academies or official bodies that attempt to regulate usage. The Turkish language reform of the twentieth century is a striking example of deliberate intervention, as thousands of words of Arabic and Persian origin were replaced within a few decades. Such cases show that planning can have real effects, particularly when it is supported by the state and the education system.

Even so, most change occurs without any central direction. Dictionaries increasingly describe how a language is used instead of prescribing how it should be used. From this perspective, grammatical rules are better understood as summaries of the conventions of a community than as laws that exist independently of its speakers.

sections.title: When Languages Disappear
paragraphs: Change is natural, but the loss of a language is a different matter. Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken today, a large proportion have few remaining speakers, and many are not being passed on to children. When parents believe that another language offers better opportunities, a language can disappear in only a few generations.

Such a loss involves more than words. A language can preserve knowledge of local plants, history and ways of understanding the world that may not be recorded elsewhere. For this reason, communities and researchers are working to document endangered languages and, in some notable cases, to bring them back into everyday use.

books.title: The Attention Economy
books.author: ODAK
books.description: Dikkat neden kıt bir kaynak haline geldi ve bunun etik sonuçları neler? Soyut, akademik bir dille yazılmış, sınav paragraflarına yakın bir metin.

sections.title: A Scarcity of Attention
paragraphs: As early as 1971, the economist Herbert Simon observed that a wealth of information creates a poverty of attention. What was then a speculative remark has since become an organising principle of the digital economy. Where earlier media businesses sold content, many contemporary platforms provide content free of charge and instead derive their revenue from the time and engagement of their users, which they in turn sell to advertisers.

This arrangement alters the incentives under which information is produced. A platform whose income depends on sustained engagement has little commercial reason to distinguish between content that is valuable to its audience and content that is merely difficult to stop consuming. Although these categories overlap, they are by no means identical, and it is in the gap between them that much of the current controversy resides.

sections.title: Designing for Compulsion
paragraphs: Critics contend that certain widely used features are engineered to exploit well-documented psychological tendencies. Variable rewards, whereby a user cannot predict when a refresh will yield something interesting, have long been known to produce persistent behaviour. Likewise, infinite scrolling removes the natural stopping points that once prompted readers to consider whether they wished to continue.

Defenders of these platforms respond that such accounts underestimate the agency of users, and that the charge of manipulation could equally be levelled at novelists who end a chapter on a moment of suspense. The analogy is instructive but imperfect. A novelist does not observe each reader's behaviour in real time, nor adjust the next chapter on the basis of millions of comparable experiments.

sections.title: Evidence and Its Limits
paragraphs: Claims about the harmful consequences of heavy use must nevertheless be treated with caution. Much of the research is correlational, so it cannot establish whether extensive use causes poorer wellbeing or whether those who are already unhappy simply spend more time online. Moreover, effects that are statistically significant in large samples are frequently small, and they vary substantially according to the type of activity and the characteristics of the individual.

Popular commentary tends to neglect these complications, just as earlier generations expressed comparable anxieties about novels, radio and television. Recognising this history should not, however, lead to complacency. That previous fears proved exaggerated does not demonstrate that present concerns are unfounded, particularly given the unprecedented capacity of current systems to personalise their appeal.

sections.title: Who Is Responsible?
paragraphs: Responses to the problem reflect differing assumptions about responsibility. Approaches centred on the individual emphasise digital literacy and self-regulation, whereas structural approaches maintain that it is unreasonable to expect individuals to resist systems refined by thousands of engineers. Regulators in several jurisdictions have accordingly begun to consider restrictions on particular design practices, especially those affecting children.

Ultimately, the question is not whether attention will continue to be competed for, since it always has been, but on what terms. A society might reasonably decide that some forms of competition for the mind require limits, in the way that it has already limited certain forms of competition for labour and for money. Determining where those limits should fall, without unduly restricting expression, remains a matter of considerable and unresolved debate.
